claim: In longer days, the florigen gene FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) is induced in specific leaf phloem companion cells in Arabidopsis.
source: In longer days, the florigen gene FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) is induced in specific leaf phloem companion cells in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Bulk nuclei RNA-seq demonstrated that FT-expressing cells in cotyledons and true leaves showed differences in FT repressor gene expression.
source: Our bulk nuclei RNA-seq demonstrated that FT-expressing cells in cotyledons and true leaves showed differences in FT repressor gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bulk RNA-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within true leaves, snRNA-seq analysis revealed that companion cells with high FT expression form a unique cluster.
source: Within true leaves, our snRNA-seq analysis revealed that companion cells with high FT expression form a unique cluster.
evidence: This is directly supported by the single-nucleus RNA-seq data and clustering analysis shown in the results.

claim: The cluster of cells with high FT expression expresses other genes encoding small proteins, including FPF1-LIKE PROTEIN 1 (FLP1) and BROTHER OF FT AND TFL1 (BFT).
source: The cluster expresses other genes encoding small proteins, including the flowering and stem growth inducer FPF1-LIKE PROTEIN 1 (FLP1) and the anti-florigen BROTHER OF FT AND TFL1 (BFT).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data showing co-expression of these genes in cluster 7.

claim: The promoters of FT and genes co-expressed with FT in the cluster were enriched for the binding motif of NITRATE-INDUCIBLE GARP-TYPE TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSOR 1 (NIGT1).
source: We also found that the promoters of FT and the genes co-expressed with FT in the cluster were enriched for the binding motif of NITRATE-INDUCIBLE GARP-TYPE TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSOR 1 (NIGT1).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis performed on the promoters of cluster 7 genes.

claim: Overexpression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 repressed FT and delayed flowering under nitrogen-rich conditions.
source: Overexpression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 repressed FT and delayed flowering under nitrogen-rich conditions, implying the roles of NIGT1s as nitrogen-dependent FT repressors.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic overexpression experiments and flowering time measurements.

claim: FT is a florigen, a mobile signaling molecule that promotes flowering.
source: The small protein FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) is a florigen, a mobile signaling molecule that promotes flowering (Corbesier et al., 2007; Tamaki et al., 2007; Mathieu et al., 2007; Notaguchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Some phloem companion cells residing in the distal parts of leaves highly express FT in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, some phloem companion cells residing in the distal parts of leaves highly express FT (Takada and Goto, 2003; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FT exhibits only a single expression peak in the evening under common laboratory long-day (LD) conditions.
source: Although FT exhibits only a single expression peak in the evening under common laboratory long-day (LD) conditions, FT is highly expressed in the morning and evening under natural light conditions (Song et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FT is highly expressed in the morning and evening under natural light conditions.
source: Although FT exhibits only a single expression peak in the evening under common laboratory long-day (LD) conditions, FT is highly expressed in the morning and evening under natural light conditions (Song et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The discrepancy between natural and laboratory conditions in FT expression can be attributed to differences in the red-to-far-red light (R/FR) ratios.
source: The discrepancy between natural and laboratory conditions can be attributed to differences in the red-to-far-red light (R/FR) ratios.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adjusting the R/FR ratio to that observed in nature is sufficient to recreate the bimodal expression pattern of FT in the lab.
source: Adjusting the R/FR ratio to that observed in nature is sufficient to recreate the bimodal expression pattern of FT in the lab (Song et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The list of differentially translated transcripts in FT-expressing cells partially overlapped with that in SUC2-expressing cells but also contained unique transcripts to FT-expressing cells.
source: We found that the list of differentially translated transcripts in FT-expressing cells partially overlapped with that in the general phloem companion cell marker gene SUCROSE-PROTON SYMPORTER 2 (SUC2)-expressing cells but also contained unique transcripts to FT-expressing cells (Takagi et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study by the same authors.

claim: FT-expressing cells are similar but different from general phloem companion cells.
source: This supports the notion that the FT-expressing cells are similar but different from general phloem companion cells (Takada and Goto, 2003; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the TRAP-seq data and supported by citations.

claim: Several FT positive and negative transcriptional regulators and proteins involved in FT protein transport were specifically enriched in FT-expressing cells.
source: Our TRAP-seq datasets showed that several FT positive and negative transcriptional regulators and proteins involved in FT protein transport were specifically enriched in FT-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by TRAP-seq data from a prior study.

claim: FPF1-LIKE PROTEIN 1 (FLP1) is highly expressed in FT-expressing cells under LD conditions with adjusted R/FR ratio (LD +FR conditions), but not under standard laboratory LD conditions.
source: We also found that a gene encoding the small protein FPF1-LIKE PROTEIN 1 (FLP1) is highly expressed in FT-expressing cells under LD conditions with adjusted R/FR ratio (hereafter, LD +FR conditions), but not under standard laboratory LD conditions (Takagi et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: FLP1 promotes flowering and initial inflorescence stem growth.
source: Further analysis revealed that FLP1 promotes flowering and initial inflorescence stem growth, suggesting that it orchestrates flowering and inflorescence stem growth during the transition from the vegetative to the reproductive stage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: FT is expressed at specific times of the day in relatively small numbers of phloem companion cells.
source: As FT is expressed at specific times of the day in relatively small numbers of phloem companion cells, we needed a method to collect the information from these rare FT-expressing cells in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about FT expression patterns.

claim: Protoplasting is not ideal for isolating highly embedded phloem companion cells efficiently.
source: However, protoplasting is not ideal for isolating highly embedded phloem companion cells efficiently (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The authors deployed single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) combined with fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting (FANS) to isolate GFP-labeled cell-type-specific nuclei at a specific time of the day.
source: To overcome these technical challenges, we deployed single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) combined with fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting (FANS) to isolate GFP-labeled cell-type-specific nuclei at a specific time of the day.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The principal component analysis (PCA) of the expression data indicated separation by tissue and targeted cell population.
source: The principal component analysis (PCA) of the resulting expression data indicated separation by tissue and targeted cell population (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The biggest difference among the bulk RNA-seq datasets was the difference between cotyledons and true leaves, rather than a cell/tissue-type difference.
source: Interestingly, the biggest difference among these datasets was the difference between cotyledons and true leaves, rather than a cell/tissue-type difference.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis.

claim: FT-expressing cells show a distinct gene expression profile compared with other cell/tissue types examined.
source: Among different cells/tissues, FT-expressing cells show a distinct gene expression profile compared with other cell/tissue types examined.
evidence: This is an observation from the bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: In true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, phloem companion cell marker genes FT, SUC2, AHA3, APL, CM3, and AAP4 showed higher expression than in the p35S:NTF line.
source: As expected, in true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, phloem companion cell marker genes FT, SUC2, AHA3, APL, CM3, and AAP4 showed higher expression than in the p35S:NTF line, and the pFT:NTF line showed strong upregulation of FT in both cotyledon and true leaves (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-E).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: The pFT:NTF line showed strong upregulation of FT in both cotyledon and true leaves.
source: As expected, in true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, phloem companion cell marker genes FT, SUC2, AHA3, APL, CM3, and AAP4 showed higher expression than in the p35S:NTF line, and the pFT:NTF line showed strong upregulation of FT in both cotyledon and true leaves (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-E).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: True leaves of the pFT:NTF line showed upregulation of other phloem companion cell marker genes such as AHA3, APL, and AAP4.
source: True leaves of the pFT:NTF line also showed upregulation of other phloem companion cell marker genes such as AHA3, APL, and AAP4; however, cotyledons of the pFT:NTF line only showed upregulation of AAP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-E), indicating some of the known vascular marker genes are more suitable for representing vascular tissues in true leaves.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Cotyledons of the pFT:NTF line only showed upregulation of AAP4.
source: True leaves of the pFT:NTF line also showed upregulation of other phloem companion cell marker genes such as AHA3, APL, and AAP4; however, cotyledons of the pFT:NTF line only showed upregulation of AAP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-E), indicating some of the known vascular marker genes are more suitable for representing vascular tissues in true leaves.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Some of the known vascular marker genes are more suitable for representing vascular tissues in true leaves.
source: True leaves of the pFT:NTF line also showed upregulation of other phloem companion cell marker genes such as AHA3, APL, and AAP4; however, cotyledons of the pFT:NTF line only showed upregulation of AAP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-E), indicating some of the known vascular marker genes are more suitable for representing vascular tissues in true leaves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: In cotyledons of the pSUC2:NTF line, CM3 and AAP4 were upregulated, but not SUC2, FT, AHA3, and APL.
source: In cotyledons of the pSUC2:NTF line, CM3 and AAP4 were upregulated, but not SUC2, FT, AHA3, and APL.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority of the genes upregulated in the cotyledons of the pSUC2:NTF line were found to be expressed in the vasculature.
source: The majority of the genes upregulated in the cotyledons of our pSUC2:NTF line were found to be expressed in the vasculature.
evidence: This is based on checking the spatial expression pattern of upregulated genes.

claim: Expression of mesophyll marker gene CAB2 was significantly lower in pSUC2:NTF cotyledon samples.
source: As expected, expression of mesophyll marker gene CAB2 was significantly lower in pSUC2:NTF cotyledon samples (padj = 1.5 x 10–4), in addition to the mesophyll cell marker RBCS1A in true leaf samples, suggesting that a significant amount of mesophyll cells was successfully removed by FANS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A significant amount of mesophyll cells was successfully removed by FANS.
source: As expected, expression of mesophyll marker gene CAB2 was significantly lower in pSUC2:NTF cotyledon samples (padj = 1.5 x 10–4), in addition to the mesophyll cell marker RBCS1A in true leaf samples, suggesting that a significant amount of mesophyll cells was successfully removed by FANS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower expression of mesophyll markers.

claim: The vast majority of differentially expressed genes within a given transgenic line did not overlap between cotyledons and true leaves.
source: Consistent with the PCA analysis, the vast majority of differentially expressed genes within a given transgenic line did not overlap between cotyledons and true leaves (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Among the transcription factors that promote FT expression, APL and VOZ1 were upregulated in true leaves of the pFT:NTF and pSUC2:NTF lines.
source: Among the transcription factors that promote FT expression, APL and VOZ1 were upregulated in true leaves of the pFT:NTF and pSUC2:NTF lines (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, a CO destabilizing factor was significantly upregulated.
source: In true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, a CO destabilizing factor was significantly upregulated (Figure 1I), in addition to TFs that repress FT expression (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, TFs that repress FT expression were significantly upregulated.
source: In true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF line, a CO destabilizing factor was significantly upregulated (Figure 1I), in addition to TFs that repress FT expression (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: True leaves of the pFT:NTF line did not show significant upregulation for most FT repressors.
source: In contrast to pSUC2:NTF true leaves, true leaves of the pFT:NTF line did not show significant upregulation for most of these FT repressors.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: The lack of FT repression appears to be crucial for specifying FT-expressing cells.
source: This lack of FT repression appears to be crucial for specifying FT-expressing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: There were far fewer expression differences in cotyledons between the pFT:NTF and pSUC2:NTF lines.
source: In contrast, there were far fewer expression differences in cotyledons between the pFT:NTF and pSUC2:NTF lines, indicating that the respective cells in true leaves have diverged more than comparable ones in cotyledons.
evidence: This is an observation from the bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: The respective cells in true leaves have diverged more than comparable ones in cotyledons.
source: In contrast, there were far fewer expression differences in cotyledons between the pFT:NTF and pSUC2:NTF lines, indicating that the respective cells in true leaves have diverged more than comparable ones in cotyledons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: FT expression and FT transport appeared to be more tightly associated in true leaves than in cotyledons.
source: Similarly, FT expression and FT transport appeared to be more tightly associated in true leaves than in cotyledons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of FT and FT transporter genes.

claim: The expression of the FT transporter gene FTIP1 is highly associated with FT expression.
source: As reported, the expression of the FT transporter gene FTIP1 is highly associated with FT expression (Takagi et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Significant upregulation of FTIP1 expression was observed in true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF and the pFT:NTF lines but not in the respective cotyledon samples.
source: Consistent with this earlier finding, among FT transporter genes, we observed significant upregulation of FTIP1 expression in true leaves of the pSUC2:NTF and the pFT:NTF lines but not in the respective cotyledon samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H-K).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In the pFT:NTF line, the genes involved in the 'regulation of reproductive process' were upregulated in both cotyledons and true leaves.
source: In the pFT:NTF line, the genes involved in the 'regulation of reproductive process' were upregulated in both cotyledons and true leaves, while the genes related to the term 'long-day photoperiodism, flowering' were only upregulated in the true leaf samples of the pFT:NTF line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The genes related to the term 'long-day photoperiodism, flowering' were only upregulated in the true leaf samples of the pFT:NTF line.
source: In the pFT:NTF line, the genes involved in the 'regulation of reproductive process' were upregulated in both cotyledons and true leaves, while the genes related to the term 'long-day photoperiodism, flowering' were only upregulated in the true leaf samples of the pFT:NTF line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A total of 1173 nuclei were captured for the pFT:NTF line and 3650 nuclei for the pSUC2:NTF line in snRNA-seq.
source: We captured a total of 1173 nuclei for the pFT:NTF line and 3650 nuclei for the pSUC2:NTF line.
evidence: This describes the snRNA-seq data collection.

claim: In total, 4823 nuclei were captured and 20,732 genes were detected, with a median of 149 genes per nuclei.
source: In total, we captured 4823 nuclei and detected 20,732 genes, a median of 149 genes per nuclei (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This describes the snRNA-seq data collection shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gene expression of the nuclei was projected in a two-dimensional UMAP as 11 different clusters.
source: Gene expression of these nuclei was projected in a two-dimensional UMAP as 11 different clusters (McInnes et al., 2018; Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The nuclei in clusters 8 and 10 showed substantially higher numbers of transcripts than other clusters.
source: The nuclei in clusters 8 and 10 showed substantially higher numbers of transcripts than other clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Nuclei with the highest FT expression resided in cluster 7.
source: We first asked which nuclei highly expressed FT. These nuclei resided in cluster 7 (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: SUC2 expression showed a far broader distribution across clusters than FT expression.
source: SUC2 expression showed a far broader distribution across clusters than FT expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The nuclei in cluster 7 significantly highly expressed 268 genes compared with the total population.
source: The nuclei in cluster 7 significantly highly expressed 268 genes compared with the total population (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Among the 268 genes highly expressed in cluster 7, FLP1 was found.
source: Among these genes, we found FLP1 (Figure 2G), a gene encoding a flowering-promoting factor acting in parallel with FT (Takagi et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2G and citation to a prior study.

claim: 202 of the 268 genes highly expressed in cluster 7 showed higher expression in FT-expressing cells than in whole companion cells in the prior TRAP-seq study.
source: 202 of the 268 genes showed higher expression in FT-expressing cells (pFT:FLAG-GFP-RPL18) than in whole companion cells (pSUC2:FLAG-GFP-RPL18) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) in the prior study, validating our single nuclei analysis.
evidence: This cross-validation with prior TRAP-seq data supports the snRNA-seq findings.

claim: FKBP12, a gene encoding a CO stabilizing protein, was expressed in cluster 7.
source: Further, FKBP12, a gene encoding a CO stabilizing protein, was expressed in cluster 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Serrano‐Bueno et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures and citation to prior research.

claim: Genes involved in 'Oxidative phosphorylation' were enriched in cluster 7.
source: Genes involved in 'Oxidative phosphorylation' were enriched in cluster 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that ATP synthesis is particularly active in nuclei belonging to this cluster (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: ATP synthesis is particularly active in nuclei belonging to cluster 7.
source: Genes involved in 'Oxidative phosphorylation' were enriched in cluster 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that ATP synthesis is particularly active in nuclei belonging to this cluster (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation genes.

claim: Genes involved in proton-generating complex I–IV and ATP synthesizing complex V in mitochondrion membrane were upregulated in cluster 7.
source: Genes involved in proton-generating complex I–IV and ATP synthesizing complex V in mitochondrion membrane were also upregulated in cluster 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that the entire ATP synthesis pathway is activated in FT-expressing nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The entire ATP synthesis pathway is activated in FT-expressing nuclei.
source: Genes involved in proton-generating complex I–IV and ATP synthesizing complex V in mitochondrion membrane were also upregulated in cluster 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that the entire ATP synthesis pathway is activated in FT-expressing nuclei.
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of ATP synthesis pathway genes.

claim: Phloem companion cells actively hydrolyze ATP to generate proton gradients to load sucrose and amino acids.
source: Since phloem companion cells actively hydrolyze ATP to generate proton gradients to load sucrose and amino acids (Hunt et al., 2023), it is plausible that FT-expressing phloem companion cells generate a substantial amount of ATP for transport.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: FT-expressing phloem companion cells generate a substantial amount of ATP for transport.
source: Since phloem companion cells actively hydrolyze ATP to generate proton gradients to load sucrose and amino acids (Hunt et al., 2023), it is plausible that FT-expressing phloem companion cells generate a substantial amount of ATP for transport.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the enrichment of ATP synthesis genes and known phloem function.

claim: Cluster 4 showed significantly higher SUC2 expression compared with other clusters, suggesting companion cell identity.
source: Like cluster 7, cluster 4 showed significantly higher SUC2 expression compared with other clusters, suggesting companion cell identity (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: The genes LTP1, MLP28, and XTH4 were upregulated in cluster 4, consistent with prior studies showing their exclusive expression in vascular tissues.
source: Moreover, the genes LTP1, MLP28, and XTH4 were upregulated in cluster 4, consistent with prior studies showing their exclusive expression in vascular tissues (particularly in the main vein) that include phloem (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C; Kushwah et al., 2020; Litholdo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures and citations to prior research.

claim: Genes encoding aquaporin were enriched in cluster 4.
source: Terms enrichment analysis found that genes encoding aquaporin were enriched in cluster 4 (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2I and supplementary figures.

claim: PIP2;6 promoter activity showed the strongest signal in the main vein.
source: To understand which part of leaf tissue consists of cluster 4 cells, we marked the promoter activity of PLASMA MEMBRANE INTRINSIC PROTEIN 2.6 (PIP2;6), an aquaporin gene highly expressed in cluster 4, using the GFP-fusion protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F and G). It showed the strongest signal in the main vein, consistent with the previous GUS reporter assay (Prado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the GFP reporter assay shown in supplementary figures and citation to prior research.

claim: The nuclei in cluster 4 are likely to be derived from phloem cells in the main vein that are active in solute transport.
source: Taken together, the nuclei in cluster 4 are likely to be derived from phloem cells in the main vein that are active in solute transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns and spatial localization.

claim: Cluster 5 is mostly composed of nuclei from the pSUC2:NTF line (464 out of 515 nuclei).
source: Cluster 5 is mostly composed of nuclei from the pSUC2:NTF line (464 out of 515 nuclei; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The nuclei in cluster 5 showed differentially expressed genes related to defense.
source: The nuclei in this cluster showed differentially expressed genes related to defense (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: MYC2, a master regulator of response to jasmonic acid (JA), and the JA biosynthetic genes LOX3, LOX4, OPR3, and OPCL1 are expressed in cluster 5.
source: Specifically, MYC2, a master regulator of response to jasmonic acid (JA), and the JA biosynthetic genes LOX3, LOX4, OPR3, and OPCL1 are expressed in cluster 5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: OPR3 is expressed in phloem companion cells and LOX3/4 in phloem.
source: These genes are known to be expressed in vascular tissues, with OPR3 expressed in phloem companion cells and LOX3/4 in phloem (Chauvin et al., 2016; Kienow et al., 2008; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This subpopulation of phloem cells appears to play pivotal roles in JA-dependent defense responses.
source: This subpopulation of phloem cells appears to play pivotal roles in JA-dependent defense responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of JA-related genes.

claim: The nuclei isolation process may have triggered wounding responses due to chopping samples before the sorting process.
source: Because these cells were not fixed, the nuclei isolation process may have triggered wounding responses due to chopping samples before the sorting process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of JA-related gene expression.

claim: Cluster 6 consisted of both phloem parenchyma and bundle sheath cells.
source: Cluster 6 consisted of both phloem parenchyma and bundle sheath cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Subclustering revealed that the nuclei in the upper part of cluster 6 expressed phloem parenchyma marker genes, and the nuclei in the lower part expressed bundle sheath marker genes.
source: Subclustering revealed that the nuclei in the upper part of cluster 6 expressed phloem parenchyma marker genes, and the nuclei in the lower part expressed bundle sheath marker genes (Kim et al., 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by subclustering analysis shown in supplementary figures and citation to prior research.

claim: The genes expressed in cluster 6 were enriched for genes functioning in sulfur metabolisms.
source: Overall, the genes expressed in this cluster were enriched for genes functioning in sulfur metabolisms (Figure 2—figure supplement 5G), including glucosinolate biosynthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5H).
evidence: This is supported by Terms enrichment analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Sulfur metabolic and glucosinolate biosynthetic genes are actively expressed in bundle sheath cells.
source: A previous study showed that sulfur metabolic and glucosinolate biosynthetic genes are actively expressed in bundle sheath cells (Aubry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Clusters 1, 2, and 3 showed expression of mesophyll cell marker genes.
source: Lastly, Clusters 1, 2, and 3 showed expression of mesophyll cell marker genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that some mesophyll cells were included during the sorting process.
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Some mesophyll cells were included during the sorting process.
source: Lastly, Clusters 1, 2, and 3 showed expression of mesophyll cell marker genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that some mesophyll cells were included during the sorting process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of mesophyll markers.

claim: Weak induction of the FT and SUC2 promoters in mesophyll cells might explain the inclusion of mesophyll cells.
source: This result might be due to weak induction of the FT and SUC2 promoters in mesophyll cells (Takagi et al., 2025).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Both FT and SUC2 genes were expressed at low levels in mesophyll protoplasts.
source: Indeed, we found both genes to be expressed at low levels in mesophyll protoplasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Using snRNA-seq combined with FANS, the authors revealed the presence of a unique subpopulation of cells with high nuclear FT expression.
source: In summary, using snRNA-seq combined with FANS, we revealed the presence of a unique subpopulation of cells with high nuclear FT expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the snRNA-seq findings.

claim: In nuclei with high FT expression, genes related to ATP synthesis were enriched.
source: In these nuclei, genes related to ATP synthesis were enriched.
evidence: This is a summary of the snRNA-seq findings.

claim: Other phloem cell clusters were identified that were enriched for genes in water transport and JA response, which were not previously reported.
source: Moreover, we identified other phloem cell clusters enriched for genes in water transport and JA response, which were not previously reported (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the snRNA-seq findings with citation to prior research.

claim: Subclustering of cluster 7 revealed three subclusters.
source: Next, we subclustered the nuclei in cluster 7, finding three subclusters (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by subclustering analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Subcluster 7.2 contained the nuclei with the highest FT expression, in addition to expression of the companion cell marker genes, SUC2 and AHA3.
source: Subcluster 7.2 contained the nuclei with the highest FT expression, in addition to expression of the companion cell marker genes, SUC2 and AHA3.
evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis.

claim: Nuclei in subcluster 7.2 contained fewer transcripts of the mesophyll marker genes RBCS1A, CAB3, and CAB2.
source: These nuclei contained fewer transcripts of the mesophyll marker genes RBCS1A, CAB3, and CAB2 (Figure 3C and D), consistent with a prior scRNA-seq study showing the negative correlation between the expression of vasculature and mesophyll cell marker genes (Torii et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 3C and D and citation to prior research.

claim: The vascular tissue located at the distal part of true leaves, where FT is expressed highly, is developmentally old, whereas veins emerging from the bottom part of leaves are developmentally young.
source: The vascular tissue located at the distal part of true leaves, where FT is expressed highly, is developmentally old, whereas veins emerging from the bottom part of leaves are developmentally young (Biedroń and Banasiak, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Subcluster 7.3 may be comprised of nuclei from developmentally younger companion cells that have not fully matured yet, whereas those in subcluster 7.2 are older and have gained a stronger companion cell identity.
source: Thus, subcluster 7.3 may be comprised of nuclei from developmentally younger companion cells that have not fully matured yet, whereas those in subcluster 7.2 are older and have gained a stronger companion cell identity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression patterns and developmental knowledge.

claim: The median number of amino acids encoded in the differentially expressed genes of cluster 7 is smaller than those in clusters 4 and 5.
source: Indeed, the median number of amino acids encoded in the differentially expressed genes of cluster 7 is smaller than those in clusters 4 and 5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The spatial expression patterns of eight selected cluster 7-enriched genes and high FT signals overlapped.
source: To validate whether high FT-expressing vascular cells co-express genes specifically upregulated in cluster 7, which encode small proteins, we selected eight such genes and generated their respective promoter fusions with H2B-tdTomato in the pFT:NTF background. The spatial expression patterns of these eight genes and high FT signals overlapped (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the confocal imaging shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: FT and cluster 7-enriched genes examined tended to express highly in the distal part of minor veins, but weakly in the main vein adjacent to the petiole.
source: FT and cluster 7-enriched genes examined tended to express highly in the distal part of minor veins, but weakly in the main vein adjacent to the petiole, showing a clear difference from the cluster 4-enriched gene PIP2;6 that is expressed highly in the main vein (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the confocal imaging shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The spatial expression patterns of FT and other cluster 7-enriched genes did not completely overlap; there were cells expressing only one of them at high levels.
source: It should also be noted that the spatial expression patterns of FT and other cluster 7-enriched genes did not completely overlap; there were cells expressing only one of them at high levels (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by the confocal imaging shown in supplementary figures.

claim: T1 pSUC2:BFT plants grown under LD +FR conditions showed severely delayed flowering compared with pSUC2:GFP control lines.
source: T1 pSUC2:BFT plants grown under LD +FR conditions showed severely delayed flowering compared with pSUC2:GFP control lines (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The result that pSUC2:BFT delays flowering under LD +FR conditions is in stark contrast to prior results obtained under standard laboratory light conditions.
source: This result is in stark contrast to prior results obtained under standard laboratory light conditions (Ryu et al., 2014), suggesting that BFT proteins might be mobile or more functionally active under natural light conditions.
evidence: This is an observation comparing current results with prior research, with citation.

claim: BFT proteins might be mobile or more functionally active under natural light conditions.
source: This result is in stark contrast to prior results obtained under standard laboratory light conditions (Ryu et al., 2014), suggesting that BFT proteins might be mobile or more functionally active under natural light conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed difference in BFT effects under different light conditions.

claim: None of the other transgenic lines overexpressing cluster 7 genes showed noticeable changes in flowering time.
source: None of the other transgenic lines showed noticeable changes in flowering time, although the leaf numbers slightly decreased in the AT1G24575 overexpressing lines.
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements.

claim: The leaf numbers slightly decreased in the AT1G24575 overexpressing lines.
source: None of the other transgenic lines showed noticeable changes in flowering time, although the leaf numbers slightly decreased in the AT1G24575 overexpressing lines.
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements.

claim: The most enriched motif in the promoters of the 268 genes differentially expressed in cluster 7 was the motif of NITRATE-INDUCIBLE GARP-TYPE TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSOR 1.2 (NIGT1.2).
source: We performed motif enrichment analysis on the promoters of the 268 genes differentially expressed in cluster 7 (Dreos et al., 2015; Meylan et al., 2020), using randomly selected 3000 genes as a control set. The most enriched motif was the motif of the NITRATE-INDUCIBLE GARP-TYPE TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSOR 1.2 (also known as HHO2, p=9.3 x 10–6) (Figure 5—source data 1)(Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Constitutive expression of NIGT1.2 significantly decreases FT expression.
source: Although the NIGT1/HHO transcription factors (TFs) are primarily known as repressors of genes involved in nitrate uptake, constitutive expression of NIGT1.2 significantly decreases FT expression (Kiba et al., 2018; Maeda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are two potential NIGT1 binding sites located within and adjacent to the shadow 1 and 2 domains (S1 and S2) in the FT regulatory region.
source: In fact, there are two potential NIGT1 binding sites located within and adjacent to the shadow 1 and 2 domains (S1 and S2) in the FT regulatory region (Adrian et al., 2010; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in supplementary figures and citation to prior research.

claim: The S1 and S2 domains are highly conserved among Brassicaceae species and important for FT transcriptional regulation.
source: These domains are highly conserved among Brassicaceae species and important for FT transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about FT regulation.

claim: The NIGT1 binding motifs reside in close proximity to the CO binding motif (TGTGNNATG, CO-responsive element, CORE).
source: Moreover, the NIGT1 binding motifs reside in close proximity to the CO binding motif (TGTGNNATG, CO-responsive element, CORE; Adrian et al., 2010; Tiwari et al., 2010), suggesting that NIGT1 binding could affect CO binding.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations to prior research.

claim: NIGT1 binding could affect CO binding.
source: Moreover, the NIGT1 binding motifs reside in close proximity to the CO binding motif (TGTGNNATG, CO-responsive element, CORE; Adrian et al., 2010; Tiwari et al., 2010), suggesting that NIGT1 binding could affect CO binding.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proximity of binding sites.

claim: Y1H screening found that NIGT1.1/HHO3, NIGT1.2/HHO2, NIGT1.3/HHO1, NIGT1.4/HRS1, and HHO5 specifically bind to the FT promoter sequence containing the S1 and S2 domains.
source: We performed a yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) screen of 1957 TFs against four tandem repeats of a short FT promoter sequence containing the S1 and S2 domains and the two NIGT1 binding sites (Bonaldi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). We found that NIGT1.1/HHO3, NIGT1.2/HHO2, NIGT1.3/HHO1, NIGT1.4/HRS1, and HHO5 specifically bind to this sequence within the FT regulatory region (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by the Y1H screening data.

claim: At the T1 generation, late flowering phenotype was observed in the pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 lines.
source: Next, we overexpressed five different NIGT1/HHO genes using the SUC2 promoter. At the T1 generation, we observed the late flowering phenotype in the pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 lines, while it appeared less clear in the pSUC2:NIGT1.1, NIGT1.3, and HHO5 (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements.

claim: Under LD +FR conditions, pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and pSUC2:NIGT1.4 transgenic plants flowered significantly later than wild-type plants.
source: Therefore, we generated T3 lines of pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and pSUC2:NIGT1.4 and measured their flowering time. Under LD +FR conditions, these transgenic plants flowered significantly later than wild-type plants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Genes specifically expressed in cluster 7, such as FT, BFT, and SAQR, were downregulated in both the pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and pSUC2:NIGT1.4 lines.
source: To test which genes were altered by the overexpression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4, we conducted RNA-seq analysis of the respective transgenic plants (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 3–6). We found that genes specifically expressed in cluster 7, such as FT, BFT, and SAQR, were downregulated in both the pSUC2:NIGT1.2 and pSUC2:NIGT1.4 lines.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FLP1 expression was decreased only in pSUC2:NIGT1.2 lines.
source: FLP1 expression was decreased only in pSUC2:NIGT1.2 lines, which might explain why pSUC2:NIGT1.2 plants exhibited a more severe late flowering phenotype than pSUC2:NIGT1.4 plants.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data.

claim: pSUC2:NIGT1.2 plants exhibited a more severe late flowering phenotype than pSUC2:NIGT1.4 plants, which might be explained by the decrease in FLP1 expression only in pSUC2:NIGT1.2 lines.
source: FLP1 expression was decreased only in pSUC2:NIGT1.2 lines, which might explain why pSUC2:NIGT1.2 plants exhibited a more severe late flowering phenotype than pSUC2:NIGT1.4 plants.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects on FLP1 expression.

claim: Co-expression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 significantly decreased the promoter activity of pFT compared with that of pFTm, while GFP did not change the pFT activity compared with pFTm.
source: To test if NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 directly regulate the FT promoter activity, we conducted the tobacco transient promoter luciferase (LUC) assay using the FT promoter (pFT) and the one with the mutations in three potential NIGT1 binding sites (pFTm) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). Our data showed that co-expression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 significantly decreased the promoter activity of pFT compared with that of pFTm, while GFP did not change the pFT activity compared with pFTm (Figure 5C), suggesting that NIGT1s directly repress FT expression level.
evidence: This is supported by the tobacco transient LUC assay shown in Figure 5C.

claim: NIGT1s directly repress FT expression level.
source: To test if NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 directly regulate the FT promoter activity, we conducted the tobacco transient promoter luciferase (LUC) assay using the FT promoter (pFT) and the one with the mutations in three potential NIGT1 binding sites (pFTm) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). Our data showed that co-expression of NIGT1.2 and NIGT1.4 significantly decreased the promoter activity of pFT compared with that of pFTm, while GFP did not change the pFT activity compared with pFTm (Figure 5C), suggesting that NIGT1s directly repress FT expression level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the LUC assay results.

claim: NIGT1.2 is expressed broadly in shoots while NIGT1.4 is expressed only in roots.
source: Consistent with our snRNA-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B), previous studies reported that NIGT1.2 is expressed broadly in shoots while NIGT1.4 is expressed only in roots (Kiba et al., 2018), suggesting that NIGT1.2 is the major player in FT regulation.
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in supplementary figures and citation to prior research.

claim: NIGT1.2 is the major player in FT regulation.
source: Consistent with our snRNA-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B), previous studies reported that NIGT1.2 is expressed broadly in shoots while NIGT1.4 is expressed only in roots (Kiba et al., 2018), suggesting that NIGT1.2 is the major player in FT regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns.

claim: Neither NIGT1.2 nor NIGT1.4 expressed highly in cluster 7.
source: Interestingly, neither NIGT1.2 nor NIGT1.4 expressed highly in cluster 7.
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNA-seq data.

claim: NIGT1s have a role to prevent the misexpression of FT and perhaps other cluster 7 genes in non-cluster 7 cells.
source: We speculate that they have a role to prevent the misexpression of FT and perhaps other cluster 7 genes in non-cluster 7 cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression patterns and functional data.

claim: Ample nitrogen prolongs the vegetative growth stage and delays flowering.
source: Ample nitrogen prolongs the vegetative growth stage and delays flowering ; however, the detailed mechanisms of this delay remain largely unknown (Sanagi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NIGT1 genes are induced under high nitrogen conditions.
source: Since NIGT1 genes are induced under high nitrogen conditions, we tested the quadruple mutant of the NIGT1 genes (nigtQ mutant) for FT and BFT expression with (+N) and without high nitrogen (–N) (Kiba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The nigtQ plants showed enhanced FT and BFT expression compared to the wild-type plants under +N but not –N conditions.
source: The nigtQ plants showed enhanced FT and BFT expression compared to the wild-type plants under +N but not –N conditions, suggesting that the NIGT1 TFs act as novel nitrate-dependent regulators of flowering (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D and supplementary figures.

claim: The NIGT1 TFs act as novel nitrate-dependent regulators of flowering.
source: The nigtQ plants showed enhanced FT and BFT expression compared to the wild-type plants under +N but not –N conditions, suggesting that the NIGT1 TFs act as novel nitrate-dependent regulators of flowering (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects under different nitrogen conditions.

claim: The nigtQ plants bolted earlier in days than WT when they grew with 20 mM NH4NO3.
source: To test if nigtQ mutations affect flowering timing under different nitrogen conditions, we transplanted 9-day-old WT and nigtQ seedlings grown on Murashige and Skoog-based media with 20 mM NH4NO3 to new media containing either 20 mM or 2 mM NH4NO3. The nigtQ plants bolted earlier in days than WT when they grew with 20 mM NH4NO3, whereas the flowering time of WT and nigtQ was almost identical under 2 mM, suggesting that NIGT1 genes delay flowering under ample nitrogen conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The flowering time of WT and nigtQ was almost identical under 2 mM NH4NO3.
source: To test if nigtQ mutations affect flowering timing under different nitrogen conditions, we transplanted 9-day-old WT and nigtQ seedlings grown on Murashige and Skoog-based media with 20 mM NH4NO3 to new media containing either 20 mM or 2 mM NH4NO3. The nigtQ plants bolted earlier in days than WT when they grew with 20 mM NH4NO3, whereas the flowering time of WT and nigtQ was almost identical under 2 mM, suggesting that NIGT1 genes delay flowering under ample nitrogen conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: NIGT1 genes delay flowering under ample nitrogen conditions.
source: To test if nigtQ mutations affect flowering timing under different nitrogen conditions, we transplanted 9-day-old WT and nigtQ seedlings grown on Murashige and Skoog-based media with 20 mM NH4NO3 to new media containing either 20 mM or 2 mM NH4NO3. The nigtQ plants bolted earlier in days than WT when they grew with 20 mM NH4NO3, whereas the flowering time of WT and nigtQ was almost identical under 2 mM, suggesting that NIGT1 genes delay flowering under ample nitrogen conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the flowering time measurements under different nitrogen conditions.

claim: There was no difference between WT and nigtQ in leaf number at bolting when grown on media.
source: However, there was no difference between WT and nigtQ in leaf number at bolting (Figure 5—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the leaf number measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The nigtQ mutation enhanced overall plant growth speed rather than developmental timing of flowering.
source: Therefore, it appears that the nigtQ mutation enhanced overall plant growth speed rather than developmental timing of flowering.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that days to bolting changed but leaf number did not.

claim: The nigtQ mutant generated slightly more leaves than WT when they flowered on nitrogen-rich soil.
source: We also have counted leaf numbers of the nigtQ at bolting on nitrogen-rich soil. The mutant generated slightly more leaves than WT when they flowered (Figure 5—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the leaf number measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The NIGT-derived fine-tuning of FT regulation is conditional on higher nitrogen conditions.
source: These results suggest that the NIGT-derived fine-tuning of FT regulation is conditional on higher nitrogen conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects under different nitrogen conditions.

claim: In young Arabidopsis plants grown in LD, true leaves show FT expression in the distal and marginal parts of the leaf vasculature, while cotyledons express FT across entire veins.
source: In young Arabidopsis plants grown in LD, true leaves show FT expression in the distal and marginal parts of the leaf vasculature, while cotyledons express FT across entire veins (Ito et al., 2012; Takada and Goto, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The true leaves, but not the cotyledons, of the pSUC2:NTF and pFT:NTF lines showed differences in the expression of FT negative regulators.
source: The true leaves, but not the cotyledons, of the pSUC2:NTF and pFT:NTF lines showed differences in the expression of FT negative regulators.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: FT expression is strongly repressed in most of the true leaf companion cells, contributing to the spatial expression pattern of FT observed in true leaves.
source: This result suggests that FT expression is strongly repressed in most of the true leaf companion cells, contributing to the spatial expression pattern of FT observed in true leaves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression of FT repressors.

claim: The cluster 7 nuclei are derived from cells that appear to be metabolically active and produce ATP, which may be used to upload sugars, solutes, and small proteins, including FT, into the phloem sieve elements.
source: The cluster 7 nuclei are derived from cells that appear to be metabolically active and produce ATP, which may be used to upload sugars, solutes, and small proteins, including FT, into the phloem sieve elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of ATP synthesis genes.

claim: FT expression levels were positively correlated with companion cell marker gene expression and negatively correlated with mesophyll cell marker gene expression.
source: Based on subclustering analysis, FT expression levels were positively correlated with companion cell marker gene expression and negatively correlated with mesophyll cell marker gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis.

claim: The observed shift from mesophyll to companion cell identity may represent the trajectory of companion cell development.
source: The observed shift from mesophyll to companion cell identity may represent the trajectory of companion cell development (Torii et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Nuclei isolated from phloem cells with high expression of aquaporin and JA-related genes were not identified in a previous protoplast-based scRNA-seq analysis targeting phloem.
source: In clusters 4 and 5, we found nuclei isolated from phloem cells with high expression of aquaporin and JA-related genes, respectively. These cell populations were not identified in a previous protoplast-based scRNA-seq analysis targeting phloem (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an observation comparing current results with prior research, with citation.

claim: These cells (with high aquaporin and JA-related gene expression) are highly embedded in the tissue and therefore practically difficult to isolate by protoplasting.
source: We speculate that these cells are highly embedded in the tissue and therefore practically difficult to isolate by protoplasting.
evidence: This is a speculation about why these cells were not identified in prior protoplast-based studies.

claim: JA biosynthetic genes such as LOX3/4 and OPR3 are highly expressed in phloem including companion cells.
source: Previous studies show that JA biosynthetic genes such as LOX3/4 and OPR3 are highly expressed in phloem including companion cells (Chauvin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013), consistent with our results.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aquaporin genes such as PIP2;1 and PIP2;6 are thought to be highly expressed in leaf xylem parenchyma and bundle sheath tissues.
source: Aquaporin genes such as PIP2;1 and PIP2;6 are thought to be highly expressed in leaf xylem parenchyma and bundle sheath tissues (Prado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cluster 6, which contains nuclei isolated from bundle sheath and phloem parenchyma cells, showed fewer expressed aquaporin genes than the cluster 4 nuclei, which also expressed SUC2.
source: However, cluster 6, which contains nuclei isolated from bundle sheath and phloem parenchyma cells, showed fewer expressed aquaporin genes than the cluster 4 nuclei, which also expressed SUC2.
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNA-seq data.

claim: The cells active in water transport exist not only in bundle sheath or xylem parenchyma cells but also in a subpopulation of phloem cells.
source: This result might indicate that the cells active in water transport exist not only in bundle sheath or xylem parenchyma cells but also in a subpopulation of phloem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of aquaporin genes.

claim: SUC2/FT-expressing vasculature cells consist of cell subpopulations with different functions within true leaves.
source: In summary, SUC2/FT-expressing vasculature cells consist of cell subpopulations with different functions within true leaves.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the snRNA-seq data.

claim: A drawback of the snRNA-seq analysis was shallow reads per nucleus.
source: A drawback of our snRNA-seq analysis was shallow reads per nucleus.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the study.

claim: The shallow reads per nucleus appears mainly due to the low abundance of mRNA in FANS-isolated nuclei from 2-week-old leaves.
source: It appears mainly due to the low abundance of mRNA in FANS-isolated nuclei from 2-week-old leaves.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of shallow reads.

claim: The average mRNA level per nucleus in the isolated samples is approximately 0.2 pg.
source: Based on our calculation, the average mRNA level per nucleus in our isolated samples is approximately 0.2 pg (3000 pg mRNA from 15,000 sorted nuclei).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data.

claim: A previous study reported that BFT driven by the SUC2 promoter does not alter flowering time.
source: Although a previous study reported that BFT driven by the SUC2 promoter does not alter flowering time (Ryu et al., 2014), our result shows that overexpression of this gene delays flowering under LD +FR conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research, with citation.

claim: The discrepancy in BFT effects on flowering time is likely due to the use of growth conditions with the adjusted R/FR ratio that mimics natural light conditions.
source: This discrepancy is likely due to our use of growth conditions with the adjusted R/FR ratio that mimics natural light conditions, as the majority of our transgenic lines showed a similar late flowering phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the discrepancy.

claim: In Chrysanthemums, a weak florigen CsFTL1 and a strong anti-florigen CsAFT are both expressed in leaves in long days.
source: There is precedent for the co-expression of florigen and anti-florigen in leaves in other plants. In Chrysanthemums, a weak florigen CsFTL1 and a strong anti-florigen CsAFT are both expressed in leaves in long days.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Short-day conditions repress CsAFT but induce the expression of a strong florigen CsFTL3 to initiate flowering in Chrysanthemums.
source: Short-day conditions repress CsAFT but induce the expression of a strong florigen CsFTL3 to initiate flowering (Higuchi, 2018; Higuchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The balance in florigen and anti-florigen expression is important for wild tomatoes to control flowering time.
source: The balance in florigen and anti-florigen expression is also important for wild tomatoes to control flowering time, and this regulation was lost in domesticated tomatoes, resulting in day-neutral flowering behaviors (Soyk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: This regulation (balance in florigen and anti-florigen expression) was lost in domesticated tomatoes, resulting in day-neutral flowering behaviors.
source: The balance in florigen and anti-florigen expression is also important for wild tomatoes to control flowering time, and this regulation was lost in domesticated tomatoes, resulting in day-neutral flowering behaviors (Soyk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the FT-homolog floral repressor TERMINAL FLOWER 1 (TFL1) is expressed at the shoot apical meristem and competes with FT for physical interaction with FD.
source: In Arabidopsis, the FT-homolog floral repressor TERMINAL FLOWER 1 (TFL1) is expressed at the shoot apical meristem and competes with FT for physical interaction with FD (Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of TFL1 is crucial for the balance between flowering initiation and stem growth because FT terminates inflorescence stem growth.
source: In addition to preventing precocious flowering, the presence of TFL1 is crucial for the balance between flowering initiation and stem growth because FT terminates inflorescence stem growth (McKim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: BFT directly binds to FD.
source: Like FT and TFL1, BFT directly binds to FD (Ryu et al., 2014), suggesting that BFT's mode of action is similar to that of TFL1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: BFT's mode of action is similar to that of TFL1.
source: Like FT and TFL1, BFT directly binds to FD (Ryu et al., 2014), suggesting that BFT's mode of action is similar to that of TFL1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity in FD binding.

claim: Loss of BFT does not affect flowering time under standard growth conditions.
source: However, unlike for TFL1, loss of BFT does not affect flowering time under standard growth conditions (Ryu et al., 2014; Yoo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The lack of a visible flowering phenotype in the bft knockout mutant might be due to the substantially lower expression of BFT compared to FT under standard growth conditions.
source: The lack of a visible flowering phenotype in the bft knockout mutant might be due to the substantially lower expression of BFT compared to FT under standard growth conditions (Ryu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The bft knockout mutant is significantly delayed in flowering under high salinity conditions where BFT gene expression is strongly induced.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the bft knockout mutant is significantly delayed in flowering under high salinity conditions where BFT gene expression is strongly induced (Ryu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: BFT appears to act as an anti-florigen under specific growth conditions, possibly including LD +FR conditions.
source: Thus, BFT appears to act as an anti-florigen under specific growth conditions, possibly including LD +FR conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects under different growth conditions.

claim: The existence of multiple specialized anti-florigens might facilitate signal integration and reduce noise in the onset of flowering and stem growth.
source: Given the complexity of natural environments, the existence of multiple specialized anti-florigens might facilitate signal integration and reduce noise in the onset of flowering and stem growth.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of multiple anti-florigens.

claim: A recent study showed that ample nitrogen availability causes phosphorylation of FLOWERING BHLH 4 (FBH4), a direct positive regulator of CO, which results in attenuation of FBH4 transcriptional activity.
source: A recent study showed that ample nitrogen availability causes phosphorylation of FLOWERING BHLH 4 (FBH4), a direct positive regulator of CO, which results in attenuation of FBH4 transcriptional activity (Sanagi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The FBH4 mechanism acts upstream of FT, whereas the NIGT1 TFs likely act as direct repressors of FT.
source: This mechanism acts upstream of FT, whereas the NIGT1 TFs likely act as direct repressors of FT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different modes of action.

claim: Multiple nitrogen-dependent mechanisms acting on FT regulation might ensure the proper balance between nutrient availability and resource allocation toward developmental transitions.
source: Multiple nitrogen-dependent mechanisms acting on FT regulation might ensure the proper balance between nutrient availability and resource allocation toward developmental transitions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of multiple nitrogen-dependent mechanisms.

claim: Unique FT-expressing phloem cells may produce multiple systemic signals to regulate plant growth and development.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that unique FT-expressing phloem cells may produce multiple systemic signals to regulate plant growth and development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: pROXY10:amiRNA-ft and pSUC2:amiR-ft lines severely delayed flowering.
source: As a result, pROXY10:amiRNA-ft and pSUC2:amiR-ft lines severely delayed flowering (in fact, pSUC2:amiRNA-ft flowered later than ft-101 mutant, likely due to the effect of the hygromycin selection plate).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: pPIP2;6:amiR-ft was comparable with the negative control pGC1:amiRNA-ft line.
source: On the other hand, pPIP2;6:amiR-ft was comparable with the negative control pGC1:amiRNA-ft line (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the flowering time measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The basal expression level of ROXY10 was much lower than that of SUC2 and PIP2;6.
source: The basal expression level of ROXY10 was much lower than that of SUC2 and PIP2;6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B); therefore, the delayed flowering phenotype of pROXY10:amiR-ft lines was not attributed to the promoter strength of genes used to drive the amiRNA.
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The delayed flowering phenotype of pROXY10:amiR-ft lines was not attributed to the promoter strength of genes used to drive the amiRNA.
source: The basal expression level of ROXY10 was much lower than that of SUC2 and PIP2;6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B); therefore, the delayed flowering phenotype of pROXY10:amiR-ft lines was not attributed to the promoter strength of genes used to drive the amiRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression level data.

claim: FT expressed in a relatively small but unique cluster 7 is biologically significant for flowering time regulation.
source: These results indicate that FT expressed in a relatively small but unique cluster 7 is biologically significant for flowering time regulation, although FT expressed in other companion cells other than cluster 7 cells may also contribute to flowering.
evidence: This is an inference based on the amiRNA knockdown experiments.
